newsitem.title: USA: U.S. House panel takes up Medicare plan.
newsitem.headline: U.S. House panel takes up Medicare plan.

text.p: The House Ways and Means Committee was expected to give bipartisan support Monday to a plan to restructure Medicare and cut its spending by $115 billion over five years.

The compromise plan, passed by a subcommittee 13-0 last week, was to be taken up late in the day. Passage would be the first concrete action in Congress to translate a five-year balanced budget plan into law.

The bipartisan cooperation stood in marked contrast to the bitter battles of two years ago when Democrats and Republicans were at war over possible changes in the popular health programme for 38 million Americans, including everyone aged 65 and older. The bill avoided major increases in Medicare premiums that people pay while expanding benefits and offering a wide array of health plan choices to recipients.

The bulk of the spending cuts would come from reducing Medicare payments to hospitals, managed care and other health providers. The legislation provided new incentives to expand Medicare managed care to rural areas and allowed doctors and hospitals to band together to form their own health networks.

Democrats at the committee session were expected to offer amendments to scale back a pilot programme for special tax-free Medical Savings Accounts (MSAs). They also wanted to defeat some Republican-backed malpractice award limits.
Both of those efforts failed in the subcommittee and Republicans were likely to beat them back in full commmittee.

Under the MSA proposal, Medicare recipients would be given set payments to be deposited in a tax-free savings account. The account would be used in conjunction with catastrophic insurance policy with a deductible of no more than $6,000.
Funds could be withdrawn from the MSA for routine medical bills. Money left over could be rolled over to the next year.

Republicans said the proposal would make seniors more cost-conscious. The administration fears the healthiest Medicare recipients would opt for MSAs, leaving sicker, more expensive seniors in the regular programme and increasing costs.

While the budget deal was expected to keep Medicare solvent for a decade, both sides acknowledged major structural changes will be needed to protect the programme in coming years as the baby boom generation reaches retirement age.
